## [0.19.0] - 2026-08-19

The **agents and transport release**. Two epics land side by side. MCP stops being the read-mostly half of Vayu: an agent can now run a whole collection in design mode or under load, start and drive mock servers and webhook inboxes, create and switch environments, read and clear the cookie jar, write a saved request's auth and every Settings field, curate its examples, and keep run history - roughly thirty new tools over routes the engine already had. Underneath, the engine gains one transport policy that every outbound path inherits, carrying manual proxies, pasted CA anchors, per-request `verifySSL` and a per-host client-certificate registry, so an internal or mTLS-protected API is callable at all. The OpenAPI work 0.18.0 started gets its follow-through - a bound spec is described rather than transferred, a document-level change is applyable, and orphaned documents are reclaimed - and the dialog primitive learns to fit on a screen. The bulk of the change is new TypeScript in the app's MCP server and new C++ in the engine's transport layer.

### Added

- **One transport policy, and a manual proxy on every outbound path.** The engine had proxy *readers* and no writer: `proxy_url` sat in two config structs that nothing ever assigned, SSE had no proxy option at all, and the only proxying Vayu did was libcurl's implicit environment pickup, which a desktop launch never sees. `TransportPolicy` is resolved from settings at the point of use and applied by one function for all three drivers, so a transport option cannot land on two paths and miss the third - which is exactly how SSE never got a proxy. Design sends, `pm.sendRequest`, load runs, collection runs, SSE streams, the OAuth token fetch, `/import/fetch` and the monitor scrape all inherit it, and the load and collection paths read it once per run because libcurl only reuses a pooled connection when its proxy config matches. Modes are `environment` (today's behaviour, named), `manual` and `off`, where off genuinely disables the env pickup; `manual` always writes the bypass list, empty or not, since libcurl consults the ambient `no_proxy` whenever `CURLOPT_NOPROXY` is unset. A refused `CONNECT` becomes `ErrorCode::ProxyError` rather than a plain receive error, read off `CURLINFO_HTTP_CONNECTCODE` - the only place a 407 survives.
- **Custom CA certificates, and `verifySSL` end to end.** A new `customCaCertificates` setting takes pasted PEM anchors, validates them, materializes a bundle beside the database and hands its path to the one applier, so the anchors reach every path the policy does. They *extend* the platform's rather than replacing them: on an OpenSSL build `CURLOPT_CAINFO` is the whole trust store, so the file is the system anchors plus the pasted ones, while Schannel and Apple SecTrust keep their OS store and the engine sets `NATIVE_CA` beside the bundle. A backend that refuses the option is named in the log rather than failing every later request with nothing saying why. `verifySSL` becomes a real column on `requests` carried through both serializers, `POST /compose`, the replay path and a Settings toggle that paints a warning while verification is off - never elided at its default, because a dropped `false` verifies the certificate the user opted out for. `curl -k` and wget's `--no-check-certificate` now import as that setting instead of being skipped, and the curl generator emits `-k` back.
- **Client certificates (mTLS) as a per-host registry.** Nothing in the engine ever set `CURLOPT_SSLCERT`, so an mTLS endpoint was uncallable. A certificate is a property of where you are calling rather than of one request - the transfer that needs it is as often a token fetch, a redirect or a script's `pm.sendRequest` - so this is a registry keyed by host and port, applied by the engine, and no request names a certificate. The private key never enters the database (paths are stored, and both are checked at write time, since an unreadable one otherwise surfaces at handshake as an SSL error that reads like "the API is broken"), one entry per host+port pair, and a match is exact with port-specific beating catch-all and no wildcards. Settings > Network & connectivity gains the card; a cert-authenticated exchange carries the matched entry through both design funnels and shows a chip on the response status bar.
- **Run a collection from MCP, in design mode or under load.** `run_collection` starts the same design-mode runner the Run Collection dialog does - steps one at a time, sharing the environment's cookie jar, honouring `pm.execution` flow control, running stored scripts, repeating per data row - and `start_load_run` takes a `scenario` block to hand the same plan to the load executor. The allowlist gate is all-or-nothing here: every step is composed by id and gated before the run row exists, so one step off the allowlist refuses the whole run with nothing sent, naming the step the engine would have reached first. Modes that cannot drive a sequence (`capacity`, `constant_rps`, any non-zero `targetRps`) are refused with the engine's own reasoning, and every argument describing a single target is refused by name beside a scenario rather than being silently unread.
- **Mock servers and webhook inboxes over MCP.** The examples-driven mock server and the webhook inbox both shipped without an agent surface, which left their one agent loop - start a listener, trigger the sender, assert on what arrived - unreachable. Twelve tools cover lifecycle, routes, captures and live editing: `update_mock_issuer` and `update_inbox_response` merge-patch a *running* service, so an agent testing retry behaviour flips the failure mode instead of destroying and recreating an issuer, which would invalidate the token URL the request under test points at. Every listener the engine binds is loopback with no host to configure, and `inboxStartPayload` never emits `bind` whatever the arguments carry. A started mock that has nothing mappable answers 404s, so the counts the engine already reports become a sentence on the result rather than something to spot in the JSON.
- **Environments, globals and the cookie jar over MCP.** An agent could merge values into an environment that already existed and nothing else. Seven tools add create, activate and delete, globals read and write, and the cookie jar's read and scoped clear, while `update_environment` gains a per-variable `{value, secret, type, enabled}` form and a `removeVariables` list. Both blobs merge through one implementation because both are replaced wholesale engine-side: a field the call did not state keeps its stored value, so a rotated secret stays masked. A variable with no stored value must carry one, so `{secret: true}` against a mistyped name is an error rather than a new empty secret; a name in both `variables` and `removeVariables` is refused, because "set it and delete it" has no correct order; and a removal that found nothing is a note, not an error, so a retried call cannot fail on its own success.
- **Saved-request parity: auth, every Settings field, and example CRUD.** `create_request` and `update_request` now take the request's `auth` block and all five Settings fields (`followRedirects`, `maxRedirects`, `httpVersion`, `stream`, `verifySSL`), on the merge-patch rule the strings already followed - which for `verifySSL` is a security rule rather than a convenience, since a defaulted `true` on an unrelated update would silently re-enable a check the user turned off. The auth input is `run_request`'s own schema re-described rather than a copy, so an agent can write back verbatim what `list_requests` handed it. Examples get the CRUD the engine has had since 0.16.0, with `origin` the one field no tool accepts: a created example is always `user`, because a claimable origin would let an agent hand its own example to the next spec sync to overwrite. `create_collection` / `update_collection` reach variables, auth and both collection scripts, and `move_item` re-parents through `POST /reorder` - atomic against a concurrent move where a plain update is not - offering `first` / `last` only and refusing a collection into its own subtree.
- **Run housekeeping over MCP.** `list_runs` fetched the first 100 rows with no parameters; it now takes the engine's filters and paging, with `type` and `status` as real enums rather than passthrough strings, because `GET /runs` ignores one it cannot parse and a typo forwarded raw would answer the unfiltered page and read as "nothing matched anywhere". `delete_run` and `set_run_baseline` land the write half that was never shipped, and `get_run_samples`, `get_run_timeseries` and `get_run_monitor` open the captured data, defaulting well under the engine's own page sizes, refusing a limit past the cap rather than clamping it, and saying in words when a page has more behind it.
- **Load-run recording knobs, OAuth 2.0 token tools and the scripting types.** `start_load_run` takes `successSamplePeriod`, `slowRequestThresholdMs`, `saveTimingBreakdown` and `comment`, each named for what the value means rather than for the engine key it maps to, and all four reach a scenario run as well, since forwarding on one path would be a knob that silently does nothing on the other. `fetch_oauth2_token`, `get_oauth2_token_status` and `clear_oauth2_token` cover the token cache under two stated rules: no tool returns access-token bytes - the engine is what applies a token, so the bytes buy an agent nothing it can use through Vayu while turning a credential into something it can carry off the machine - and the `authorization_code` grant is refused before the engine is called, because `acquire_token` answers a cache hit before it looks at the grant. `vayu://scripting/types` re-serves the `.d.ts` the app's editor loads.
- **The bound contract as a gate, from the Run dialog and from MCP.** The engine has read `failOnSchemaError` off `POST /runs` since 0.18.0 and no Vayu surface could write it, so the feature was reachable only by hand-writing a raw request. The Run Collection dialog gains a **Fail steps on schema errors** switch, off as the engine is and sent only when on, hidden for a load run because only the design-mode runner demotes a step; `run_collection` takes the same flag; `start_load_run` declares it purely so it can be refused by name, since an argument a schema does not name is stripped before the handler runs and would vanish in silence.
- **Describe a bound spec instead of transferring it.** Opening the Spec tab pulled the whole stored document - 12 MB for Stripe's, 9.7 MB for GitHub's - to paint a source line and a fetch date, rendering a fallback claim and a flashing `0 of 0` while it did. `GET /specs/:id/meta` answers id, source, fetch time, hash and byte count with the content and both indexes absent rather than emptied, narrowed from the full serialization so the two cannot drift. Export, the import dialog's bound-spec match and Sync's Check still read the whole document, each on the action that needs it.
- **`POST /import/fetch` takes a caller-stated `maxBytes`, under a transport ceiling.** The transfer is cut off while the body arrives rather than checked after it has been buffered whole, and the refusal is its own `ResponseTooLarge` answered as a 413 naming the bound. The spec paths pass the live `maxSpecDocumentBytes`, which also moves a `$ref` bundle's per-file refusal to where the bytes arrive; the format-agnostic URL box passes nothing and gets the engine's ceiling rather than restating a number that could drift from it.
- **HTML in an OpenAPI description renders, sanitized in the same pipeline.** Stripe's official document writes every operation description as HTML, which is spec-legal - OpenAPI descriptions are CommonMark and CommonMark admits inline HTML - so the Info tab showed the tags as literal text. Raw HTML is parsed and immediately pruned against a schema derived from the component's own element allow-list; the order is the security property, because sanitizing first sanitizes a tree the payload is not in yet. The schema keeps `href` on an anchor and no other attribute - `class` least of all, since the cheap attack on a renderer that keeps it is a full-viewport overlay rather than a script - passes http(s) only, and strips `script` and `style` whole instead of unwrapping their text onto the screen.

### Changed

- **The dialog primitive fits on the screen and comes in two widths.** A dialog taller than the viewport was centred on a box it did not fit, clipped top and bottom at once with nothing to scroll, and the footer is the half that goes - which makes the primary action unreachable by pointer, and only by pointer, since Tab still reaches it, which is how it survived across thirteen call sites. Panels now cap at 85vh with a scrolling `DialogBody` band; putting the scroll on the panel is the one-line version and the wrong one, because the corner close button is absolute inside it and would scroll away exactly when the dialog grew long enough to need a visible way out. Widths had drifted to five values across eleven call sites, so the same kind of dialog came out a different size depending on who wrote it; there are now two, `lg` for a form or a decision and `xl` for a dialog holding something with a shape of its own.
- **The request Settings tab and the engine enum card are built on the shared settings rows.** Both were hand-rolled copies of shapes the settings primitives already define, which is how a copy stops receiving the primitive's fixes - the request tab set its section headings in the same type as the control labels under them, so six sibling lines read where three groups were meant. Sections are `Eyebrow` labels a tier above the rows now, a section holding a single row *is* that row, and two primitives gained the label and `aria-describedby` wiring this tab was giving up, so the whole settings screen gets it too.
- **A run's report and a request's response are bounded before an agent reads them.** Neither engine cap covers a tool result - `maxResponseBodyBytes` bounds load runs only and `maxTraceBodyBytes` is sized for the database - so an ordinary page fetch came back as 1.3M characters and exceeded the tool-result limit outright, handing the agent an error instead of a response. Bodies are held to 32 KB inline, the number this codebase already uses for how much of a body an automated reader gets, with the truncation flag and the true size beside it; a cut raw body nulls its parsed twin rather than handing back in full the bytes it just said were dropped. `get_run_report` also holds its traces to 96 KB in total, since at 100 rows truncation is no longer the binding constraint - non-passing steps spend the budget first, matching the store's own rule about which steps matter, and the first trace is always embedded so a design run's single-row report never comes back empty.
- **A collection's header counts the subtree it acts on.** `CollectionDetail` counted only the requests a collection owns directly, while the mock toggle in the same header serves the subtree, the Run dialog runs it and the export walks it - so a spec-bound root read "GitHub v3 REST API - 0 requests" above a mock serving a thousand routes. The sidebar is deliberately unchanged: its `(N)` is the count of direct child rows, tied to `aria-setsize` and to what expanding reveals.

### Fixed

- **A collection run's step keeps the assertions it made, and a pre-request assertion is listed where it is counted.** A run held every `pm.test` result in the exchange and spent them on one summary error line, so a step could be `failed` with an error naming an assertion beside a Tests list that did not contain it, and a passing step showed no evidence its assertions had run at all. The step trace now carries the scripts node design mode already stores and the step frame carries the tallies - two numbers on the frame because the tick ring is fixed-size and a script may make hundreds of assertions, the list on the stored row. Both scripts' assertions are listed, in execution order, each naming its source, because an assertion made before the request went out is a different claim from one about the response.
- **A load run's test outcomes are readable after the run.** The engine writes `testValidation` into every load-run report and stores the named failures on a synthetic result row, and exactly one surface read either: the live dashboard, mounted only while a run is being watched. Reopened from History - precisely where someone audits results - a run that failed 13 of 100 sampled test executions was indistinguishable from one that asserted nothing, while the failure row itself rendered in Samples as a status-0 card with no request behind it. The card moves into History's Overview beside the schema block it is the assertion counterpart of, and the run-view outcome chips now read the engine's exact whole-run totals rather than tallying stored rows, which thinning drops.
- **Bound data cells are disclosed where they actually live.** "Its rows are never saved anywhere" was true of the file and the contract and false of every cell that reached a request: a collection run stores each step's exchange, and bind-before-auth builds the Authorization header out of the row's own values, so a credentials CSV run on the strength of that claim leaves every iteration's password in SQLite and on screen. Eight surfaces now separate the row *set* (never stored, count alone) from a bound value (stored with the request that carried it, expiring with the run), a warning names the bound rows over the collection-run step list, and a source guard pins the retired claims so they cannot come back.
- **The data-contract audit reads the credentials a run binds, and the Run dialog resolves the contract through the chain.** Since credentials bind per iteration, a collection whose contract declares `user` and `password` for a basic-auth pair read "declared but not referenced" - the reading that gets a working column deleted. The walk now covers the credentials the engine visits and no more, resolving what a request actually sends through `inherit` first, because in the flagship case they live on the collection. The Run dialog resolved the contract by the target's own id while the documented rule is nearest-declared-ancestor, so running a sub-collection under a declaring parent bound rows but offered no pre-fill and no column diff.
- **The Data tab re-reads the declared file instead of asking for it again**, and every re-read enforces the row cap. The tab whose whole purpose is the file-versus-contract comparison was the one surface that never read the file, so it rendered "Declared from users.csv" and "Nothing to compare yet" on one screen. A file that has moved now degrades softly - the declared name struck through with the read failure after it - and the shared reader enforces `maxScenarioDataRows`, which the picker applied before a run and the three re-read paths did not, leaving the engine's 400 as the only feedback.
- **A re-bind clears the stamps it orphans, and unreachable spec documents are reclaimed.** Binding stamped the requests that matched the new document and said nothing about the rest, so re-binding left every non-matcher carrying identity from the old - and coverage resolves stamps by `operationId` first, so such a stamp does not go unread, it claims whichever operation of the *new* document shares the id. Separately, nothing ever deleted a document that stopped being reachable: every sync mints one and moves the binding off the last, so weekly syncs of a 12 MB spec stranded ~600 MB a year. One lifetime rule now governs it - a document lives while a collection binds it or a retained run names it - swept by the pass that releases those run references, sparing anything written in the last ten minutes because that is a bind in flight.
- **A document-level spec change is applyable, and a method edit survives a sync.** A document whose only change is a response schema, a new status or its `servers` block produced zero diff entries and Apply was disabled on exactly that shape, so the commonest contract change of all was permanently unapplyable while the UI truthfully said the document had changed. Every apply now stores the document and the ticks decide which request rows ride along. `method` was the other hole - not compared, never a checklist row, never flagged as edited, and written unconditionally - so a user who changed an imported GET to HEAD had it reverted by any applied change.
- **Deleting an imported example is a decision that lasts.** A spec sync replaces every imported example of a request it touches, a rename being enough, so a deleted one came back on the next sync while the Examples panel promised the opposite. The row is kept as a tombstone the refresh honours and every ordinary read filters out, so the list route, a mock server, an export and a `PUT` all behave exactly as though it were gone. The identity is the *status*, not the name: an imported example is the document's account of one response code, while its name carries a description that moves whenever the document rewords it.
- **Four silent losses in the OpenAPI import path.** `servers[0].url` is resolved before it becomes `{{baseUrl}}` - variable defaults substituted, a relative URL resolved against where the document was fetched from - where a templated URL used to survive literally into every request line and fail at connect. A cookie parameter and a `requestBody` declaring only media types Vayu cannot model are counted rather than dropped, the second having returned the same answer as *no body at all*, so a binary upload imported as a bodyless POST reporting nothing skipped. The single-document cap is enforced before the parse, instead of a whole over-cap file being fetched, parsed and previewed and first refused at apply. And unquoted `swagger: 2.0`, which YAML loads as the number 2, is no longer "Unrecognised format".
- **Untagged operations get folders, and a `default` response stops reading as an error.** A document whose operations declare no tags - as Stripe's 568 do not - imported as one flat list. An untagged operation now takes a folder named after the first meaningful path segment, stepping over a version, an `api` mount point and a whole templated segment, with the strategy disclosed in the preview because a folder tree the document never spelled out must not read as one it did. Every vendor spec declares the catch-all `default` on every operation, which the shared skip counter reported in destructive red beside the one warning that could be acted on; it has its own counter at informational severity now, while malformed keys keep the warning.
- **The export writes what is stored, not part of it.** A truncated example body entered the contract as a quoted fragment indistinguishable from a complete example - the skeleton direction gaining the most, since it derives a schema from an example body and would have stated the fields one capture reached as the whole response shape. The subtree walk took no descend predicate, so a collection bound to a *different* spec nested underneath contributed its requests, whose stamps collide on generator-common names and rewrote operations here. And assembly ran in a render-time memo, re-running from scratch on every format toggle, so a 12 MB document froze the window with nothing on screen to say why.
- **Coverage says how many statuses a row is hiding.** Two capped lists shared one drop counter, so a code past both caps was counted twice while a code the undeclared list still carried counted as dropped with the row showing it. The number is now a subtraction over what was actually emitted, which lets the row paint the union of the two lists - an undeclared code past the seen cap arrived in one alone and was dropped from the display while the count beside it did not account for it. Undeclared statuses, capped counts and off-range responses all render now, where the engine had computed them and the app typed them and nothing showed them.
- **A deleted run stops being restored into an open tab.** The last-design-run family was the one per-request run key with no plural prefix, so nothing that changes the run set without naming a request could reach it - and a run id gives no way back to the request it belonged to. Deleting a request's most recent design run, from History, over MCP or by clearing the history, left that tab restoring the response of a run the sidebar no longer lists. The MCP invalidator gained the same three prefix families the app's own mutations clear, plus a run-id scope hint that drops a deleted run's report, samples and series rather than marking them stale, since both are held indefinitely and went on rendering under an open History tab.
- **A tooltip hint has to read on the tooltip.** The primitive painted its hint in a token tuned against the canvas, which measures 1.04:1 on the default accent scheme against the tooltip's filled surface - so the mock-server row printed its URL in grey on blue, and the URL is the one thing in that tooltip a reader has to read. De-emphasis on a filled surface has to be an alpha of the foreground that already reads on it, which two other sites had worked out for themselves while the primitive never received it. Guarded three ways: the class read off the rendered element, the ratio measured against every accent scheme, and a scan of all 17 tooltip blocks in the app so the next hand-written one cannot repeat it.
- **The title bar can be dragged by the slack right of the search bar**, where the right-hand cluster had set `no-drag` on a wrapper spanning an entire grid column rather than on the control inside it - a dead strip most visible on Windows and macOS, where the reserved overlay padding widens it further.
- **The Dock's running-services indicator counts mock servers**, the third of the three local services the engine hosts, so a bound loopback listener holding a port contributed zero and the Dock disagreed with the drawer it opens.

### Security

- **Header text no header line can hold is refused, from every origin.** A composed `{{variable}}` was substituted into a header name or value with nothing on that path scanning the result, so an environment value holding `ok\r\nX-Admin: true` did not sit in the header - it ended the line and made the remainder a header nobody wrote. A multipart form-field name went to the wire as written, the same forgery one layer down in the part's own header block. The rule now has one definition and three layers, each named for what it can still say: the bind-time refusal names the column and the row, `POST /compose` refuses with a 400 naming the variable - the last layer that knows which one carried the byte - and the pre-send gate covers every other origin at once, including a script's assignment to `pm.request.headers`, an auth credential, an import and a payload posted straight to `POST /execute`. Refusal rather than repair, for the reason an XML comment is one: a header has no escape for a line break, so every candidate encoding either changes the value or leaves the line ended. A NUL, which `curl_slist_append` silently truncates the line at, is covered by the same gate.
- **A per-call "skip TLS verification" is refused by name.** `run_request` declares `verifySSL` only so that `false` is answered with a refusal pointing at the two routes that leave a record - trusting the authority under Settings > Network & connectivity, or storing the flag on the request the app then shows as accepting any certificate. The toggle it replaces would have been a global permission granted once for one dev box and held for the rest of the session, where the stored field is per request and revocable.

### Internal

- **The engine test suite runs multi-process on Linux and macOS.** ~2000 tests were 100% serial because ~40 fixtures open a scratch database by relative filename in a shared working directory. Each test process now gets a private directory instead of 40 fixtures being touched, which cuts the Linux leg from 3-5 min to about a fifth of that at `-j8`. Windows stays serial deliberately: measured on CI, per-test durations there are bimodal with the slow band being exactly the fixtures that open a database, so concurrent SQLite file I/O costs more than the concurrency saves - ~37 min against a ~6 min serial baseline.
- **Releases compile against a warm cache again.** The cache-warm workflow only ever configured the engine, on the reasoning that a version bump re-preprocessed every translation unit; 0.18.0 moved the version behind a declaration, so the precondition was met and the payoff never collected - every release still compiled cold at a 0% hit rate. The warm job now compiles through sccache, triggers on a version change, fails loudly if it processed zero compile requests, and is graded against the release workflow's own preset and launcher config.
- **A custom CA is verified on a wire, and the claim that said we already did is corrected.** The cited test set a nonexistent bundle path and asserted the option was accepted - it proved the backend does not refuse the option and nothing more. A generated CA and leaf are now served from a real TLS server and driven through the ordinary send path in four cases, because the happy path alone would pass on any machine with a permissive store. The material is generated per run rather than checked in, so the suite goes red on a change rather than on a date. Where a backend demands revocation information a freshly minted CA cannot publish, the positive cases skip on the backend's own error text rather than on the host platform, and print it.
- PR CI moves lint, format and type-check onto their own job off the suite's critical path, and shards the Windows app suite across two runners with a gate that unions what the shards actually ran against the file list - a sharded suite is green when each shard is green, which is also true of a shard that ran nothing. Elsewhere: a dead copy of the engine's error-code enum that had drifted four members behind is deleted rather than wired up, and several docs are corrected to name the drawer, the surface and the cap they describe.
